titre: A Bethlehem Dealer First Judged the Qumran Manuscripts Worthless
accroche: In 1947, a dealer turns down ancient scrolls found by shepherds; a cobbler keeps one, and three others go for seven Jordanian pounds.
contenu_vulgarise:
Between November 1946 and February 1947, the Bedouin Muhammed edh-Dhib is looking for a stray goat in a cave on the northwestern shore of the Dead Sea, near the site of Qumran, in the West Bank. With his cousin Jum’a Muhammed and Khalil Musa, he finds jars containing seven scrolls of skin and papyrus, among them the Isaiah scroll. The shepherds first hang them from a tent peg, then show them to their families.

## The mechanism

What follows depends on no expertise at all. A first dealer, Ibrahim ’Ijha, in Bethlehem, judges them worthless and turns them down. The shepherds are then pointed to Khalil Eskander Shahin, known as “Kando,” a cobbler and part-time antiquities dealer. Kando keeps one scroll for himself; the Bedouin sell three others to a dealer for seven Jordanian pounds, about twenty-eight dollars at the time. The remaining scrolls change hands again before reaching anyone who knows what they hold.

Scholarly recognition comes by a comparable detour. John Trever, of the American School of Oriental Research, compares the handwriting of the scrolls with that of the already known Nash Papyrus and dates the whole to Antiquity. Millar Burrows announces the discovery on April 11, 1948. The cave itself is found only at the end of a search conducted in reverse: on January 28, 1949, the UN observer Philippe Lippens and Captain Akkash el-Zebn of the Arab Legion finally locate it, making a proper excavation possible under the direction of Gerald Lankester Harding and Roland de Vaux.

The search then continues for nearly ten years. It results in a collection of 981 manuscripts from eleven caves around Qumran, discovered between 1946 and 1956 (a twelfth cave would be identified in 2017). Their dating, established by cross-checking paleography, radiocarbon and bronze coins found on the site, places the whole between the 3rd century BCE and the First Jewish–Roman War, in 68 CE.

## The shift

It was not the excavation that saved the Dead Sea Scrolls, but the chain of chance events that carried them from a dealer who saw nothing in them to a cobbler who sensed something. For months, one of the most important bodies of material ever found on the history of ancient Judaism and the origins of Christianity passed through hands unaware of its nature, until one man with no archaeological training decided not to let it leave.

The lesson is not about luck alone. It is that the value of an archaeological object is never readable on the object itself: a shriveled scroll of skin looks like any old leather, as long as no one knows what to look for. The site of Qumran, for its part, yielded its last caves only in 2017, seventy years after the first find: what remains to be discovered presents itself no more as self-evident than what has already been found.

repere.texte: The eleven caves excavated around Qumran between 1946 and 1956 yielded 981 distinct manuscripts, dated between the 3rd century BCE and 68 CE; a twelfth cave was identified in 2017.

carte.punch: One dealer judged the Dead Sea Scrolls worthless. A cobbler kept one.
carte.idee: In 1947, shepherds find ancient scrolls near Qumran. A first dealer turns them down; a cobbler keeps one and three others go for twenty-eight dollars. It will take another year for scholars to grasp their significance.

quiz.question: Why does the dating of the Qumran manuscripts not rest on a single method?
choix: Because paleography, carbon 14 and the site’s coins cross-check each other for a more secure range
Because the scrolls bear written dates that contradict one another
Because carbon 14 is ineffective on leather and papyrus
Because each cave had to be dated by a different method
quiz.explication: Three independent methods (historical dating of the writing, radiocarbon, bronze coins found on the site) converge on the same range, from the 3rd century BCE to 68 CE. A single method alone would leave a wider margin of uncertainty; carbon 14, on the contrary, works well on these organic materials.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What allowed researchers to place the first scrolls found by the shepherds in time, before any scientific dating of the site?
choix: Comparing the scrolls’ handwriting with that of the already known Nash Papyrus
The shepherds’ direct testimony about the age of the cave
A dated inscription on the Isaiah scroll itself
The Jordanian administrative records for Cave 1
quiz_supplementaire.explication: John Trever compared the letterforms of the scrolls with those of the Nash Papyrus, already dated, to propose a plausible antiquity before any excavation of the site. None of the other three options matches what the sources report.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Cave 1 have to be found a second time, in January 1949?
choix: Because the shepherds who found it had not kept its exact location for the researchers
Because an earthquake had altered the terrain between 1947 and 1949
Because the Jordanian authorities had banned access to the area for two years
Because the shepherds themselves had sealed the cave back up
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The scrolls circulated through the antiquities trade before researchers looked for the original cave, which the shepherds had not pointed out precisely. It was located only on January 28, 1949, by a UN observer and an officer of the Arab Legion.
